Stroke increased after 65 minutes; mortality rose markedly after 40 minutes

Stroke threshold first

found that occurrence of stroke increased after 40 minutes of circulatory arrest, and the mortality rate increased markedly after 65 minutes of circulatory arrest.

explanation.text: RCP was clearly effective in **maintaining cerebral hypothermia**, giving ==continuous cooling of the whole head==, and in **preventing air** from reaching the terminal vessels of the brain.

Prevents air reaching the terminal vessels of the brain
May **delay** acidosis in the ischemic brain
Lower mortality and stroke rates (479 patients)

questions.stem: A basic hypothesis underlying hypothermic circulatory arrest is that a **safe duration** of arrest exists. According to this hypothesis, which describes a safe period of circulatory arrest?

choices.text: Absence of functional derangement, even if structural changes are present
A duration directly proportional to the temperature during arrest
Absence of early derangements, regardless of late findings
A duration that is independent of the temperature during arrest
Absence of detectable functional or structural derangement, early or late

explanation.text: A safe period means ==no detectable functional **or** structural organ derangement==, in the **early or late** postoperative period.

items: There is a **safe duration** of circulatory arrest.
Its length is **inversely related** to the temperature of the organism during arrest (colder -> longer).
Safety is judged by **both function and structure**, **early and late** after operation.

explanation.title: Structure counts, even without symptoms
explanation.text: Structural derangements **without apparent functional correlates** are of concern, particularly in the **central nervous system**, because they imply a **loss of neurologic reserve** that may matter later in life.
A safe period of circulatory arrest is characterized by absence of detectable functional or structural organ derangements in the early or late postoperative period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 30

choiceNotes.a: Structural derangements without apparent functional correlates are of concern (especially in the CNS) because they imply a **loss of neurologic reserve**.
choiceNotes.b: The safe duration is **inversely** related to temperature during arrest.
choiceNotes.c: A safe period requires absence of derangements in the **early or late** postoperative period.
choiceNotes.d: The safe duration is hypothesized to be **inversely related** to temperature, not independent of it.

questions.stem: One hypothesis holds that the magnitude of reduction in oxygen consumption relates **directly** to the safe duration of circulatory arrest. Why would a close numeric relationship between the two over a wide temperature range be surprising?

choices.text: Oxygen consumption increases as body temperature falls
Other phenomena during arrest, such as no-reflow, cause damage
Oxygen consumption falls to zero once the body is below 20°C
Tissue oxygen stores sustain metabolism throughout the arrest period
Oxygen consumption cannot be used as an index of metabolic activity

explanation.text: The V̇O~2~-to-safe-time link is ==only a hypothesis==. Other phenomena occur during arrest, notably **regional vascular occlusion** in the brain (and probably all organs) leading to the **no-reflow phenomenon**.

steps.label: so
steps.text: Available **energy stores** maintain cell viability through the ischemic arrest

explanation.title: Why the link may break
explanation.text: **No-reflow** is an obstructive lesion of the microcirculation that prevents local reperfusion and leads to additional damage **after** the general circulation of blood has been reestablished.
It is only a hypothesis that a numeric relationship exists between V̇O~2~ and safe circulatory arrest time at any given temperature.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.e: V̇O~2~ **is** considered a measure of metabolic activity; its decrease by hypothermia is an index of the reduction of metabolic activity.
choiceNotes.a: Energy requirements, reflected in part by V̇O~2~, are **reduced** during hypothermia.
choiceNotes.c: V̇O~2~ is **not reduced to near zero** even at temperatures close to 0°C.
choiceNotes.d: For all practical purposes, tissue and cellular **stores of oxygen do not exist**.

questions.stem: Experimental data relating whole-body oxygen consumption to body temperature in surface-cooled animals were reanalyzed with several mathematical models. Which model best fits these data, and also the relation between temperature and **cerebral oxygen consumption during CPB in humans**?

choices.text: A log-log relation
The van't Hoff law
The Arrhenius equation
A linear equation
A hyperbolic equation

explanation.text: The ==van't Hoff law== best fits the combined surface-cooling data and is considered the **most appropriate model**; it also best fits **cerebral** oxygen consumption during CPB in humans.

explanation.caption: Models of oxygen consumption (Box 2.1)
head: Model
What it expresses
rows: Log of reaction rate **directly** related to temperature; rate rises **2–3 times per 10°C**
Log of rate inversely proportional to the reciprocal of **absolute** temperature; **S-shaped** curve with an asymptote at high temperatures
Also tested on the data; not the best fit

explanation.text: At physiologic temperatures, biochemical systems operate only on the **upswing** of the S-shaped Arrhenius curve, so, over a relatively small temperature range, the relation is expressed by the **van't Hoff law**.

explanation.title: Fig. 2.1
explanation.text: The van't Hoff regression of whole-body V̇O~2~ in surface-cooled dogs has a slope indicating a **Q~10~ of 2.7**.

choiceNotes.e: The hyperbolic equation in Box 2.1 relates V̇O~2~ to **perfusion flow rate**, not to temperature.

questions.stem: Box 2.1 defines **Q~10~** so that when T~1~ − T~2~ is 10°C, Q~10~ is simply the ratio of the metabolic rates k~1~/k~2~. Applying this definition to a tissue with a Q~10~ of **2**, if its metabolic rate at 37°C is taken as 100%, its metabolic rate at **27°C** is

explanation.text: This is a direct application of the definition: for a 10°C difference, **Q~10~ = k~1~/k~2~**. With Q~10~ = 2, the rate at 27°C = rate at 37°C ÷ 2, so cooling 37°C -> 27°C ==halves== the rate: 100% ÷ 2 = **50%**.
**Q~10~** is the multiple by which the reaction rate changes per **10°C** change in temperature; by the van't Hoff law the rate increases **two to three times** for a 10°C rise.

explanation.title: Q~10~ values in the source
items: Tissue slices and isolated organs: about **2** on average (differs from tissue to tissue)
Human whole body, heating: about **1.9**
Surface-cooled infants: estimated **1.9 to 4.2**
Surface-cooled dogs (Fig. 2.1): **2.7**

explanation.text: If T1 − T2 is 10°, then Q10 is simply the ratio of k1 to k2 (metabolic rates at each temperature).
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 31, Box 2.1

choiceNotes.b: 25% corresponds to a Q~10~ of **4** (100 ÷ 4); with Q~10~ = 2 a single 10°C fall gives 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.
choiceNotes.d: 67% corresponds to a Q~10~ of about **1.5** (100 ÷ 1.5); with Q~10~ = 2 the rate at 27°C is 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.
choiceNotes.e: 80% corresponds to a Q~10~ of **1.25** (100 ÷ 1.25); with Q~10~ = 2 the rate at 27°C is 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.
choiceNotes.a: 20% corresponds to a Q~10~ of **5** (100 ÷ 5); with Q~10~ = 2 the rate at 27°C is 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.

questions.stem: Whole-body oxygen consumption measured before and after **heating** gives a Q~10~ of about 1.9. If **cooling** yields a Q~10~ clearly greater than 1.9, what may this indicate?

choices.text: Tissue oxygen stores are being used up during cooling
True tissue oxygen requirement rises as the body cools
Vasodilatation has improved oxygen access to the tissues
Oxygen delivery is limited by an inadequate flow rate
Metabolic activity has ceased at the lower temperature

explanation.text: A Q~10~ **greater than 1.9** with cooling may mean the fall in V̇O~2~ is partly ==supply-limited==: oxygen delivery compromised by an **inadequate flow rate**.

explanation.title: Why heating shows the true requirement

steps.label: ensures
steps.text: Access of oxygen to the tissues

steps.label: so
steps.text: Q~10~ about **1.9** probably = **true tissue oxygen requirement**

explanation.title: Whole-body data may mislead
explanation.text: Only areas whose **microcirculation is still perfused** can consume oxygen, so whole-body data could **underestimate true oxygen demand**; part of the fall may come from shutting down the microcirculation or from arteriovenous shunting.
A Q10 greater than 1.9 associated with cooling may indicate that oxygen delivery has been compromised by inadequate flow rate.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.a: Tissue and cellular oxygen stores are **trivial**, so there are essentially no stores to use up.
choiceNotes.b: Energy requirements are **reduced** by hypothermia; a high Q~10~ suggests limited delivery, not a higher requirement.
choiceNotes.c: Vasodilatation is the effect of **heating**, which ensures oxygen access and gives the lower Q~10~ of about 1.9.
choiceNotes.e: V̇O~2~ is **not reduced to near zero** even at temperatures close to 0°C; metabolic activity continues.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes how **glutamate** contributes to neuronal injury during cellular energy depletion, such as cerebral ischemia during circulatory arrest?

explanation.text: When energy is depleted, the **energy-dependent synaptic reuptake** of glutamate fails; ==glutamate accumulates==, overexcites its receptors, **intracellular calcium rises**, and neurons are injured and die.

steps.text: Neuronal injury and death (**necrosis and apoptosis**)

explanation.text: **Glutamate** is the major transmitter mediating synaptic excitation in the mammalian central nervous system; this process was seen in experimental animals after **2 hours** of circulatory arrest.

Experimentally, **apoptosis** (programmed cell death) has been demonstrated in the neocortex after hypothermic circulatory arrest (piglets, 90 minutes at 19°C), with damaged neurons seen **8 to 72 hours after reperfusion**.
Resulting overaccumulation of glutamate leads to excessive excitation of the glutamate receptors, leading to an increase in intracellular calcium and eventual neuronal cell injury and death.

questions.stem: In a clinical series of 161 patients undergoing descending thoracic and thoracoabdominal aortic operations with hypothermic CPB and circulatory arrest, how did the risk of **paraplegia or paresis** relate to the duration of (hypothermic) spinal cord ischemia, up to 138 minutes?

choices.text: It exceeded 15% once ischemia lasted beyond 90 minutes
It was zero up to 60 minutes and then increased
It rose steadily with each additional 15 minutes of ischemia
It stayed low and constant regardless of the ischemic interval
It rose sharply once ischemia exceeded 60 minutes

explanation.text: With hypothermia, the prevalence of paraplegia or paresis ==remained constant and below 3.5%== for ischemic intervals of up to **138 minutes**.

items: The spinal cord is **less susceptible** to ischemic injury than the brain: no trunk or limb deficits after arrest of **up to 60 minutes** in infants, children and adults.
Hypothermia also gives important spinal cord protection during ischemia from **aortic clamping**.
Series: mean arrest **38 minutes** (range 8–62); relationship with duration P = .98 (Fig. 2.7).

explanation.title: Surgical message
explanation.text: Under hypothermia, **duration of spinal cord ischemia** (up to 138 minutes) did not change the paraplegia risk in this series.
The spinal cord is less susceptible to ischemic injury than the brain
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 40

choiceNotes.c: Risk remained **constant** (P for the relationship = .98).
choiceNotes.e: Risk stayed constant (and below 3.5%) for hypothermic ischemic intervals up to 138 minutes.
choiceNotes.a: Prevalence remained **less than 3.5%** throughout.
choiceNotes.b: The risk did not change with duration; it remained constant and below 3.5%.

questions.topic: Renal Function and Structure: Experimental Studies
questions.stem: Which statement about **hypothermia and the kidney** during circulatory arrest is supported by experimental studies in the source?

choices.text: Scattered renal cell loss causes a marked loss of renal function
The colder the better: renal damage after arrest fell steadily below 15°C
Hypothermia does not lengthen the safe circulatory arrest time of the kidney
After surface cooling to 18°C–20°C, 30 minutes of arrest caused late renal changes
Temperatures below 15°C may harm the kidney (least damage at 15°C)

explanation.text: Renal derangement after 90 minutes of arrest was ==least at 15°C== (fewer than at lower or higher temperatures), suggesting that **temperatures below 15°C may damage the kidney**.

head: Experiment
Finding
rows: Dog, surface cooling to 18°C–20°C, **90 min** arrest
explanation.caption: Hypothermia prolongs the kidney's safe arrest time

items: At any temperature, the kidney's safe arrest time is **longer than the brain's** and **shorter than the liver's**.
Scattered renal cell death probably causes **no detectable loss of function**; this may not be true in the brain.

explanation.text: This suggests that temperatures less than 15°C may damage the kidney.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 41

choiceNotes.b: After 90 minutes of arrest, derangements were **fewer at 15°C** than at either **lower** or higher temperatures.
choiceNotes.c: Hypothermia **prolongs** the safe circulatory arrest time for the dog kidney.
choiceNotes.d: **Ninety** minutes of arrest after surface cooling to 18°C–20°C produced **no** late morphologic changes.
choiceNotes.a: Scattered cell loss probably causes **no detectable** loss of renal function (unlike the brain).

questions.topic: Renal Function and Structure: Studies in Humans
questions.stem: An infant repaired with 40 minutes of hypothermic circulatory arrest at 18°C has **adequate hemodynamics** but develops severe oliguria about 12 hours postoperatively. Which mechanism does the source implicate?

choices.text: Damaging effects of CPB, e.g. free hemoglobin and circulating toxins
Low cardiac output, the only cause of renal failure after arrest
Glutamate excitotoxicity in the renal tubules
Ischemic renal injury caused by the 40-minute arrest itself
Renal tubular apoptosis mediated by caspase 3 and caspase 8

explanation.text: When oliguria occurs despite adequate hemodynamics, ==damaging effects of CPB== must be implicated, for example **free hemoglobin and circulating toxins**.

steps.text: Arrest ≤ 60 min at 18°C–20°C does **not** damage the kidney (experimental)

branches.label: primary
branches.text: **Low cardiac output** before and after arrest

steps.text: Oliguria from about **12 h** postoperatively; renal failure

items: Free hemoglobin has been found in the **renal tubules** of some patients at autopsy.
Surface-induced arrest: **4 deaths (3%)** from renal failure among 130 patients.
Adults (distal arch, descending and thoracoabdominal aorta, mean 14.5°C, mean 38 min): dialysis in **2.6%**; **none** of 18 with preoperative creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL needed dialysis.

explanation.text: Free hemoglobin has been found in the renal tubules of some of these patients at autopsy.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 41

choiceNotes.d: Experimentally, **60 minutes** of arrest at 18°C–20°C causes no morphologic or functional renal damage, so the arrest alone does not explain it.
choiceNotes.e: Caspase-mediated apoptosis is described in the **brain neocortex** of piglets, not as a cause of renal failure.
choiceNotes.b: Low output is the **primary** cause, but severe oliguria can develop when hemodynamics **appear adequate**.
choiceNotes.c: Glutamate excitotoxicity is a **neuronal** mechanism in the source, not a renal one.

questions.stem: A surgeon plans **60 minutes** of hypothermic circulatory arrest at a nasopharyngeal temperature of **18°C**. According to the source's synthesis of safe arrest duration, what outcome should be expected?

choices.text: Evident functional damage in at least 70% of patients
Mostly structural damage; functional damage in only 10%–20%
No structural damage, but functional damage in most patients
Essentially complete safety in nearly all patients
Permanent functional deficits in most patients

explanation.text: After ==60 minutes at 18°C==, most patients have some **structural** evidence of damage, but only about **10%–20%** have evident **functional** damage, often transient.

head: Arrest at 18°C (nasopharyngeal)
Expected (Fig. 2.9)
rows: Safe in **at least 70%**; damage likely **structural**, without permanent functional sequelae
Most: some **structural** damage; **10%–20%** evident **functional** damage, often transient
explanation.caption: Probability of safe circulatory arrest

explanation.title: Think in probabilities
explanation.text: Safe arrest is best expressed as a **probability** of no structural or functional damage at a given temperature, not as an absolute value; the curves at 37°C, 28°C and 18°C are estimates, not rigorously derived.

Individual vulnerability varies widely and cannot yet be predicted from genetic or phenotypic profiles; early Mayo Clinic experience suggested **45 minutes** as the maximum safe duration even at a nasopharyngeal temperature of 20°C.

Most patients will have some structural evidence of damage from 60 minutes of arrest, but only about 10% to 20% will have evident functional damage, and in many of them, the manifestations will be transient.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 42

choiceNotes.d: Essentially complete safety is **not** portrayed for 60 minutes: most patients will have some structural evidence of damage.
choiceNotes.e: Only about **10%–20%** will have evident functional damage, and in many it is **transient**.
choiceNotes.a: About 10%–20% will have evident functional damage; **70%** relates to essentially complete safety at **45 minutes**.
choiceNotes.c: The reverse: **most** have structural evidence of damage; only a **minority** have functional damage.

questions.stem: When deciding whether to use hypothermic circulatory arrest for a given operation, why must the team weigh it against **alternative perfusion strategies**?

choices.text: Circulatory arrest removes the need for a long period of CPB
Poor surgical exposure makes an inaccurate repair less likely
Arrest damage likely adds to damage from the long CPB it requires
Continuous CPB, at any temperature, carries no potential for organ damage
Genetic or phenotypic profiles now identify who will tolerate long arrest

explanation.text: The damage uniquely caused by circulatory arrest is ==likely additive== to that caused by continuous CPB, because a **long period of CPB** is required when arrest is used.

children: With or without low flow: own risks
Inaccuracy more likely with poor exposure

explanation.title: Options exist
explanation.text: Perfusion strategies other than circulatory arrest are available for **essentially all** clinical cardiac surgical problems.
the damage uniquely caused by circulatory arrest is likely additive to the damage caused by continuous CPB because a long period of CPB is required when circulatory arrest is used
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 42

choiceNotes.d: Continuous CPB at normothermia or with moderate or deep hypothermia has **its own potential** for damaging organ systems.
choiceNotes.e: State-of-the-art medicine is **not yet capable** of defining such profiles to identify individual vulnerability.
choiceNotes.a: A **long period of CPB is required** when circulatory arrest is used.
choiceNotes.b: Inaccuracies are **more** likely when surgical exposure is poor.

questions.stem: During CPB, some systemic venous blood is allowed to return to the right atrium, pass through the lungs, and be ejected by the left ventricle into the aorta. This **partial CPB** has long been known to be better tolerated than total CPB. What is the **most likely explanation**?

choices.text: Avoidance of systemic heparin anticoagulation
Need for a lower total perfusion flow rate
Lower nonphysiologic shear stress in the arterial pump
Continuation of at least some pulmonary blood flow
Avoidance of hemodilution by the priming fluid

explanation.text: Partial CPB is better tolerated than total CPB; the reasons are not clearly defined, but ==continued pulmonary blood flow== is the likely explanation.

head: Total CPB
Partial CPB
rows: **Some** returns to the right atrium and right ventricle
Blood passes the lungs -> left atrium -> **left ventricle ejects** into the aorta

explanation.text: The body is unaccustomed to the **absence of any appreciable pulmonary blood flow** and to only minimally pulsatile aortic pressure, two abnormalities of total CPB.

explanation.title: Used on purpose
explanation.text: During cooling and rewarming, partial CPB produces some arterial pulsation **and some pulmonary blood flow, with its favorable effect**.
Partial CPB has long been known to be better tolerated than total CPB. Reasons for this have not been clearly defined, but continuation of at least some pulmonary blood flow is a likely explanation.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 43

choiceNotes.c: Shear stress is one of the general complexities of CPB; it is not the explanation offered for the better tolerance of partial CPB.
choiceNotes.e: Hemodilution is not offered as the reason; the most likely explanation is continued **pulmonary blood flow**.
choiceNotes.a: The patient is anticoagulated with heparin **before CPB is established**; this is not what distinguishes partial CPB.
choiceNotes.b: Flow rate is not offered as the reason; the likely explanation is ongoing **pulmonary blood flow**.

questions.stem: During CPB, virtually all humoral and cellular components of the inflammatory response are **acutely activated**. What is the **principal cause** of this activation?

choices.text: Systemic heparin anticoagulation before bypass
Systemic hypothermia during the perfusion period
Hemodilution of plasma albumin by the priming fluid
Loss of pulsatile aortic pressure during bypass
Blood passage across nonendothelial foreign surfaces

explanation.text: Blood has always passed through **endothelium-lined channels**; during CPB it crosses ==nonendothelial foreign surfaces==, which the organism recognizes as “nonself,” and inflammation is activated.

steps.label: activates
steps.text: Virtually **all humoral and cellular** components of inflammation (and probably some specific immune responses, at least initially)

explanation.text: Other things blood does **not naturally** do on CPB: contain **gaseous and particulate emboli** and experience **nonphysiologic shear stresses**. The general **stress response** of surgery and trauma also occurs to a major degree.

explanation.title: Why it matters after surgery
explanation.text: These features make the patient who has undergone CPB a **unique organism, at least for a few days**; a detailed knowledge of the post-CPB state is necessary for optimal postoperative care.
Throughout evolution, blood has passed only through channels lined with endothelial cells, but during CPB, it is passed across nonendothelial foreign surfaces.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 43

choiceNotes.b: Hypothermia of even moderate degree appears to **blunt** some of the damaging effects of CPB.
choiceNotes.c: Hemodilution lowers colloid osmotic pressure and favors fluid shift into the interstitium; it is not the cited trigger of inflammation.
choiceNotes.d: Minimally pulsatile pressure is a separate abnormality of CPB; inflammatory activation is attributed to **foreign-surface contact**.
choiceNotes.a: Heparin is given to anticoagulate the patient; activation is linked to blood recognizing foreign surfaces as **“nonself.”**

questions.stem: During total CPB, physiologic variables fall into groups according to who controls them. Which variable is **directly controlled externally** by the perfusion team?

choices.text: Temperature of the perfusate
Systemic vascular resistance
Total body oxygen consumption
Mixed venous oxygen levels
Lactic acidemia and pH

explanation.text: Perfusate (and patient) **temperature** is one of the variables ==under direct external control== during total CPB.

explanation.caption: Three groups of variables during total CPB
head: Group
Examples
rows: Total systemic blood flow (“cardiac” output); input pressure waveform; systemic venous pressure; pulmonary venous pressure; hematocrit and chemistry of the initial perfusate; arterial O~2~, CO~2~ and nitrogen levels; temperature of perfusate and patient
Systemic vascular resistance; total body VO~2~; mixed venous O~2~ levels; lactic acidemia and pH; regional and organ blood flow; organ function
All components of **inflammation**, incited by foreign surfaces recognized as “nonself”

explanation.title: Classic confusion
explanation.text: Flow and temperature are **set**; resistance, oxygen consumption and venous oxygen levels are **responses** of the patient.
During total CPB, many physiologic variables are under direct external control, in contrast to the situation in intact humans.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 43

choiceNotes.b: Systemic vascular resistance is determined only **in part** by the controlled variables and **in large part by the patient**.
choiceNotes.c: Total body oxygen consumption belongs to the group determined in large part by the patient.
choiceNotes.d: Mixed venous oxygen levels are determined in large part by the patient, not set directly.
choiceNotes.e: Lactic acidemia and pH are partly determined by the controlled variables but largely by the patient.

questions.topic: Controlled Variables: Arterial Output to the Patient
questions.stem: An arterial **roller pump** has been adjusted so that it is **too nonocclusive**. What is the main consequence?

choices.text: Its output becomes independent of resistance
Its flow is not maintained as resistance varies
Trauma to the formed elements of blood is increased
Its output becomes markedly pulsatile
Its stroke volume rises during hypothermia

explanation.text: A roller pump that is too nonocclusive is ==unable to maintain the same flow== against the wide range of resistances (pressure differentials of **30–300 mmHg**) from the arterial cannula and systemic vascular resistance.

head: Setting
Consequence
rows: More trauma to the formed elements of blood
Cannot maintain the same flow against the range of resistances

explanation.title: How it is set
explanation.text: With the pump-oxygenator fully primed, the system is pressurized to **300 mmHg** on an onboard manometer and the roller heads are adjusted to allow a **slight pressure drop over 1 minute**.

explanation.title: Tubing in the cold
explanation.text: During hypothermia **Tygon** tubing decreases in elasticity and filling volume (stroke volume slightly falls); **silicone rubber** tubing does not, so it may be used in the pump head when hypothermia is required.
When they are occlusive, trauma to the formed elements in blood is increased; when they are too nonocclusive, they are unable to maintain the same rate of flow against the wide range of resistances
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.c: Increased trauma to formed elements occurs when roller pumps are **occlusive**.
choiceNotes.d: The roller pump generates a **relatively nonpulsatile** flow.
choiceNotes.e: During hypothermia, Tygon tubing loses elasticity and filling volume, so stroke volume slightly **decreases**.
choiceNotes.a: The reverse: a too-nonocclusive roller pump **cannot maintain** the same flow against the wide range of resistances (pressure differentials of 30–300 mmHg).

questions.topic: Controlled Variables: Arterial Output to the Patient
questions.stem: A controlled vortex (centrifugal) pump is used as the arterial pump. Why must an **ultrasonic flow meter** be placed on the arterial or venous line?

choices.text: Its output is pulsatile, so the console cannot average the flow
It is set nearly occlusive, so tubing wear alters its output
Its flow varies with inflow and outflow resistance at a given rpm
Its tubing stiffens in hypothermia and reduces its stroke volume
It cannot transmit air, so bubble detection relies on the meter

explanation.text: In contrast to the roller pump, ==rpm of the controlled vortex pump cannot be used to estimate flow==, because its flow varies with resistance to inflow and outflow; an **ultrasonic flow meter** is required.

steps.text: Resistance into or out of the pump changes

steps.label: so
steps.text: **Ultrasonic flow meter** on the arterial (output) or venous (input) line

explanation.title: Also used for
explanation.text: Closed-chest support with central or peripheral arterial and venous cannulation, termed **cardiopulmonary support (CPS)**.
Therefore, in contrast to the roller pump, revolutions per minute (rpm) of the controlled vortex pump cannot be used to estimate flow.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: The reason given is that vortex-pump flow changes with **resistance to flow into and out of the pump**, so rpm cannot estimate flow.
choiceNotes.b: The occlusion setting applies to the **roller** pump; the vortex pump is **nonocclusive**.
choiceNotes.d: That describes **Tygon tubing in a roller pump head**.
choiceNotes.e: Like the roller pump, the vortex pump **can transmit air bubbles** from the venous to the arterial lines.

questions.topic: Controlled Variables: Arterial Output to the Patient
questions.stem: During CPB with a controlled vortex (centrifugal) arterial pump, the arterial line is **accidentally clamped completely**. What happens?

choices.text: Flow continues, and line pressure rises until a connector gives way
Flow continues at the set rate because the pump speed is unchanged
Flow stops at once, and line pressure then rises without limit
Flow stops at once, and line pressure rises no higher than about 500 mmHg
Flow stops only when inflow line pressure falls to about −500 mmHg

explanation.text: With a vortex pump, complete arterial line occlusion makes ==flow cease immediately==, but line pressure rises **no higher than about 500 mmHg**, so tubing rupture or connector failure is unlikely.

explanation.caption: Built-in limits of the controlled vortex pump
head: Situation
Result
rows: Output line pressure reaches about **500 mmHg**
Inflow line pressure falls to about **−500 mmHg**

explanation.title: Safety
explanation.text: This pressure ceiling is why it is **unlikely that the tubing will rupture or a junction connector will give way**.
If the arterial line becomes completely occluded, either intentionally or by accident, flow immediately ceases, but pressure in the arterial line will rise no higher than 500 mmHg.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: Because pressure rises no higher than about 500 mmHg, it is **unlikely** that the tubing will rupture or a connector give way.
choiceNotes.b: Vortex-pump flow varies with resistance; with complete occlusion **flow immediately ceases**.
choiceNotes.c: Pressure in the arterial line rises **no higher than 500 mmHg**.
choiceNotes.e: That describes obstruction on the **inflow** side; complete outflow occlusion stops flow immediately.

questions.topic: Controlled Variables: Arterial Output to the Patient
questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares how the controlled vortex pump and the roller pump handle **air**?

choices.text: A vortex pump cannot transmit air bubbles to the arterial line
A roller pump breaks air into microbubbles; a vortex pump pumps gross air
Air causes far more blood trauma in the vortex pump than in a roller pump
A vortex pump traps air, so its flow can be estimated from rpm
Air in a vortex pump breaks into microbubbles; a roller pump will pump gross air

explanation.text: Air entrapped in a vortex pump ==breaks down into microbubbles== that eventually pass out of the pump, whereas a **roller pump will pump gross air** presented to it, with potentially disastrous consequences.

explanation.title: Do not over-trust the vortex pump
explanation.text: It still **can transmit air bubbles** from the venous to the arterial lines.
air entrapped in a vortex pump breaks down into microbubbles that eventually pass out of the pump; a roller pump will pump gross air presented to it with potentially disastrous consequences.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.a: Like the roller pump, the vortex pump **can transmit air bubbles** from the venous to the arterial lines.
choiceNotes.b: This is reversed: it is the **roller** pump that pumps gross air presented to it.
choiceNotes.c: Blood trauma is **similar** in controlled vortex and roller pumps.
choiceNotes.d: Vortex-pump rpm **cannot** be used to estimate flow; a flow meter is needed.

questions.stem: A regulated and monitored vacuum is applied to the venous reservoir, and a **roller pump** is used as the arterial pump. What is the **most important** advantage of this arrangement?

choices.text: Output and input pressures can be varied independently
Venous negative pressure rises automatically if the cannula is occluded
It requires larger venous cannulae but less priming volume
The reservoir must sit well below the patient
It allows the venous reservoir to be removed from the circuit

explanation.text: A regulated vacuum on the venous reservoir is the **ideal** method of venous drainage; most importantly, with an arterial roller pump the ==output and input pressures are uncoupled== and can be varied independently.

explanation.center: Regulated vacuum on the venous reservoir

children: Patient and machine at about the same level
Negative pressure does not exceed the set level if the cannula occludes
Negative pressure can be varied as needed
Arterial and venous pressures uncoupled (roller pump)

explanation.title: With a vortex arterial pump
explanation.text: The venous vacuum **reduces the outflow pressure** of the nonocclusive vortex pump, so **higher rpm** is needed to keep flow constant.
Most importantly, the two pressures (i.e., output pressure to the patient and input pressure from the patient) are uncoupled and can be varied independently with an arterial roller pump.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.d: With a regulated vacuum, patient and machine can be **at or near the same vertical level**, shortening the venous line.
choiceNotes.e: VAVR uses a **hard-shelled venous reservoir** with a vacuum regulator.
choiceNotes.b: With a regulated vacuum the negative pressure **does not rise above the controlled level** if the cannula becomes occluded.
choiceNotes.c: VAVR permits **smaller** venous cannulae (and smaller reservoirs, shorter tubing, low prime).

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: For a cardiac operation through a small incision, the team plans **vacuum-assisted venous return** (VAVR) using a hard-shelled venous reservoir and a vacuum regulator on wall suction. Which is the recognized **disadvantage** of this technique?

choices.text: Greater use of blood products
More microemboli at high vacuum
Need for larger venous cannulae
Larger circuit priming volume
Lower hematocrit during bypass

explanation.text: The disadvantage of VAVR is a ==potential increase in microemboli at higher vacuum settings==.
Typical setup: a **hard-shelled venous reservoir** plus a vacuum regulator on wall suction set at **−40 to −60 cm H~2~O**.

explanation.title: Where it helps most
explanation.text: Smaller cannulae, smaller reservoirs, shorter tubing and low prime make VAVR of considerable value in **infants** and for operations **through small incisions** in children and adults.
The disadvantage of VAVR is a potential increase in microemboli at higher vacuum settings.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.c: VAVR permits **smaller** venous cannulae.
choiceNotes.d: VAVR **reduced** priming volume (2.0 ± 0.4 L to 1.4 ± 0.4 L in the Cleveland Clinic study).
choiceNotes.e: VAVR **increased** hematocrit both on bypass and immediately postbypass.
choiceNotes.a: VAVR **reduced** blood product use (from 39% to 19% of patients).

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: During vacuum-assisted venous return, a ventricular drainage catheter attached to a roller pump rotating at high rpm is suddenly removed from the heart, pulling a large volume of air into the hard-shelled venous reservoir. If the reservoir is **not adequately vented**, what is the danger?

choices.text: Sudden severe hemodilution from the vent circuit
The vacuum rises without limit and collapses the venae cavae
Blood and then a column of air can be pushed up the venous line into the heart
The arterial roller pump output falls because the pressures are coupled
A vortex arterial pump delivers gross air into the aorta

explanation.text: A sudden increase of air into an inadequately vented hard-shell reservoir can ==push blood followed by a column of air up the venous return tubing and into the heart==.

steps.text: Vent on a roller pump at **high rpm** is removed

steps.label: pulls
steps.text: Large volume of **air** into the hard-shell reservoir

steps.label: drives
steps.text: Blood, then a **column of air**, retrograde up the venous line **into the heart**

explanation.title: Safeguards that resulted
explanation.text: Such complications have occurred; they led to **alarms that detect positive reservoir pressure** and **one-way (duckbill) valves** that relieve it.
If the air pulled into the venous reservoir is not adequately vented, it can push blood followed by a column of air up the venous return tubing and into the heart.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 44

choiceNotes.b: With a regulated vacuum the negative pressure does not rise above the controlled level; the danger here is **positive** reservoir pressure.
choiceNotes.d: With an arterial roller pump, venous and arterial pressures are **uncoupled** under VAVR.
choiceNotes.e: The danger described is **positive reservoir pressure** pushing blood and then air **retrograde** up the venous line, not arterial air from a vortex pump.
choiceNotes.a: The danger described is **positive reservoir pressure** driving air retrograde, not hemodilution.

questions.stem: Venous return to the pump-oxygenator is by **siphon (gravity) drainage**. What is its **most important** disadvantage?

choices.text: It works only with 18F to 20F venous cannulae
It generates a very wide range of negative pressures
It is unaffected by large boluses of air in the venous line
Its reservoir increases the priming volume
It is complex, unreliable, and expensive

explanation.text: Most importantly, siphon drainage needs a ==reservoir, which increases the priming volume==; it is otherwise simple, reliable, effective, and inexpensive.

explanation.caption: Three ways to generate venous negative pressure
head: Method
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Patient–pump level difference; narrow pressure range; interrupted by air; **reservoir -> larger prime**; 28F–32F cannulae
Same level, short line, low prime; pressure capped; pressures uncoupled
Effective; 18F–20F cannulae; peripheral and minimally invasive use
Must control the gradient at the cannula tip

explanation.text: Most importantly, the need for a reservoir increases the filling (priming) volume of the pump-oxygenator. It is, however, simple, reliable, effective, and inexpensive.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 45

choiceNotes.e: Siphon drainage is **simple, reliable, effective, and inexpensive**.
choiceNotes.a: Gravity drainage requires **28F to 32F** catheters; 18F–20F suits venous pumping with a vortex pump.
choiceNotes.b: It generates a **relatively narrow range** of negative pressures in the operating room.

explanation.text: Blood volume = 1000 × 0.08 × 10 = **800 mL**; red cell volume = 800 × 0.36 = **288 mL**; with a blood-free prime, HCTpm = 288 / (800 + 400) = ==0.24==.

f (blood volume fraction of weight)

explanation.text: If the calculated hematocrit is in the desired range, a **blood-free prime** is used; if lower than desired, an appropriate amount of blood or packed red cells is added.
where f is the proportion of body weight attributable to blood volume; f = 0.08 for infants and children up to 12 years of age, f = 0.065 for older patients, and wt is weight in kg.

questions.stem: A randomized trial **failed to find a favorable effect** from adding homologous albumin to the prime in adults. Which mechanism best explains this?

choices.text: CPB raises microvascular permeability, so albumin leaks out
Hemodilution raises the colloid osmotic pressure of plasma
Extracellular fluid expands more slowly with hemodilution
Homologous albumin reduces microvascular permeability
Albumin concentration is unaffected by hemodilution

explanation.text: During CPB ==microvascular permeability to macromolecules increases==, so administered albumin leaks into the interstitial fluid and works against the Starling relationships.

items: An **allergic response** to homologous albumin also raises permeability
Other colloids (e.g., **hydroxyethyl starch**) have not been conclusively shown to help
Keeping albumin normal in patients (often elderly) with low albumin **remains arguable**

Long-acting total α-blockade lasting about 8 to 10 hours
Antifibrinolytic action that reduces bleeding
Short-acting α-blockade needing a repeat dose for rewarming
β-blockade to slow the heart during cooling

explanation.text: ==Phenoxybenzamine== is a **long-acting α-receptor blocker** that produces total α-blockade for **8 to 10 hours** in infants and children.

head: Phentolamine
Phenoxybenzamine

1 mg/kg about 15 min before CPB, and at the beginning of rewarming after arrest

questions.stem: A single dose of **methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg** is given at the onset of CPB. Which effect is supported by evidence?

Effective osmotic diuresis from the prime
Less complement-mediated leukocyte activation
Impaired tissue perfusion during CPB
An increase in extracellular water after CPB

items: Improve **tissue perfusion**
Lessen the rise in **extracellular water**
In **piglets**, protect the brain during hypothermic CPB and circulatory arrest
Clinical benefit **controversial**

explanation.text: Regimens: **methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg** or **dexamethasone 1 mg/kg**, single dose at the onset of CPB, **not repeated**.

choices.text: 3.0 L/min/m^2^, to match his larger body size
2.5 L/min/m^2^, as for any patient at 28°C or more
2.2 L/min/m^2^, because higher flow improves oxygenator performance
1.0 L/min/m^2^, as is adequate at 18°C–20°C
1.8–2.0 L/min/m^2^, to avoid high flow through the oxygenator

explanation.text: For adults with a BSA of **2.0 m^2^ or more**, a flow of ==1.8–2.0 L/min/m^2^== may be chosen to avoid the disadvantage of **high flow through the oxygenator**.

items: More **blood trauma** in the oxygenator
More **gaseous emboli** with a bubble oxygenator
Larger **pressure gradient across the arterial cannula** -> cavitation, blood trauma, bubbles

questions.topic: Changes During CPB: Total Systemic Blood Flow
questions.stem: During CPB at conventional flow rates, the **mixed venous oxygen saturation is high**. Which interpretation is correct?

choices.text: It proves that the capillary bed is evenly perfused
It does not ensure cellular oxygenation if perfusion is uneven
It confirms that every tissue is receiving adequate oxygen
It shows that whole-body oxygen consumption is at requirement
It excludes lactic acidemia and metabolic acidosis

explanation.text: A high mixed venous PO~2~ or saturation ==does not mean cellular oxygenation is satisfactory==; an oxygen consumption at or near the whole-body requirement does.

steps.label: with Q and CaO~2~ fixed
steps.text: Mixed venous O~2~ **rises as VO~2~ falls**

steps.label: when the capillary bed is unevenly perfused
steps.text: Perfused capillaries are farther from many cells -> those cells go **hypoxic**

steps.label: amounts to
steps.text: A **shunt** of arterial blood into the venous system (sometimes half the total flow)

explanation.title: More flow is not the cure
explanation.text: If VO~2~ is below usual levels at conventional flow, increasing flow **probably will not** increase it: the fault is in the **capillary bed or at the cellular level**.

In this case, the distance between perfused capillaries and many tissue cells increases, and these cells do not obtain their oxygen requirement. This amounts to a shunt of arterial blood into the venous system.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 49

choiceNotes.c: A high mixed venous level does **not** mean cellular oxygenation is satisfactory; poorly perfused tissue may be hypoxic.
choiceNotes.d: Within the conventional flow range, mixed venous saturation is **inversely related** to oxygen consumption.
choiceNotes.e: Underperfused capillary beds produce **lactic acidemia and metabolic acidosis** despite these indices.
choiceNotes.a: Mixed venous oxygen **rises** when the capillary bed is unevenly perfused, as in a shunt.

questions.topic: Changes During CPB: Arterial Pressure Waveform
questions.stem: During cooling on CPB without a pulsatile pump, the team wants a **pulsatile arterial waveform**. How can this be achieved?

choices.text: Set the arterial roller pump fully occlusive
Fibrillate the heart and vent the left ventricle
Leave caval tapes off and let the left ventricle eject
Lower the pump flow until arterial pressure becomes pulsatile
Tighten the caval tapes and raise the venous reservoir vacuum

explanation.text: Pulsation can be achieved by ==partial CPB==: with no caval tapes, arterial flow is temporarily increased over venous return (or venous tubing partly occluded) so the **left ventricle ejects**.

steps.text: No tapes; arterial flow > venous return (or venous line partly occluded)

steps.label: so
steps.text: **Left ventricular ejection** adds to systemic flow

steps.label: giving
steps.text: Somewhat **pulsatile** arterial flow + some **pulmonary** blood flow

children: Partial CPB, during cooling and rewarming

explanation.title: Only if the heart can cope
explanation.text: Used whenever cardiac action is **vigorous enough to prevent overdistention** of the heart.
In other words, pulsation is achieved by partial CPB. This mechanism is used during cooling and rewarming whenever cardiac action is sufficiently vigorous to prevent overdistention of the heart.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 50

choiceNotes.e: Pulsation comes from **partial CPB**: caval tapes are left off and atrial filling is increased.
choiceNotes.a: The roller pump gives relatively **nonpulsatile** flow; full occlusion only increases blood trauma.

questions.topic: Changes During CPB: Arterial Pressure Waveform
questions.stem: Which conclusion about **pulsatile versus nonpulsatile** flow during CPB is best supported?

choices.text: Pulsatile flow has been proven superior in infants
Nonpulsatile flow at 80 mmHg caused subendocardial ischemia in dog hearts
Pulsatile flow energy is usually reported as energy-equivalent pressure
Evidence that it importantly reduces CPB ill effects is insufficient
A randomized trial in moderate hypothermia found lower lactate with pulsatile flow

explanation.text: There is ==insufficient evidence== that pulsatile flow importantly reduces the ill effects of the relatively short CPB needed for most cardiac surgery.

head: Evidence
Finding
rows: Vascular resistance ↑, red cells aggregate, renal function impaired, renin released, cellular hypoxia -> metabolic acidosis
**No significant differences**; no evidence of better microcirculatory perfusion
Nonpulsatile at **50 mmHg** -> subendocardial ischemia; at **80 mmHg** none with either
Faster cooling/rewarming, more urine; **difficult to interpret**

explanation.title: Where it might matter
explanation.text: Pulsatile flow could prove beneficial at **lower flows** or in **desperately ill high-risk** patients (low cardiac output, acidosis, renal failure).

Currently, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that pulsatile flow from the pump-oxygenator importantly reduces the ill effects of the relatively short periods of CPB required for cardiac surgery in the great majority of patients.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 50

choiceNotes.e: Singh and colleagues found **no significant differences** in VO~2~, lactate, vascular resistance, urine flow, or thermal gradients.
choiceNotes.a: An advantage in infants is **possible but not proven**; the supporting study is difficult to interpret.
choiceNotes.b: Subendocardial ischemia occurred with nonpulsatile flow at **50 mmHg**; at **80 mmHg** neither mode caused it.
choiceNotes.c: There is an **almost universal failure** to describe pulsatile energy properly, such as by energy-equivalent pressure.

questions.topic: Changes During CPB: Systemic Venous Pressure
questions.stem: During **total CPB**, how should systemic (central) venous pressure be managed?

choices.text: Raise it with extra prime volume to improve organ perfusion
Use the smallest cannulae that fit snugly in the cavae
Lower it by increasing systemic blood flow
Keep it at 10–15 mmHg to ensure good venous return
Keep it close to zero, and no more than 10 mmHg

explanation.text: There is no physiologic advantage to a CVP above zero during total CPB; keep it ==close to zero, and certainly not more than 10 mmHg==, to minimize extracellular fluid increase.

explanation.caption: Equation 2-2: Pv = f(Q · viscosity / cannula size, tubing size, venous negative pressure)
head: Raises venous pressure
Lowers venous pressure
rows: Larger **venous cannulae** (their cross-sectional area and length are the main fixed factors)

explanation.title: With small cannulae
explanation.text: Reduce systemic blood flow or apply **suction to the venous return** (vacuum-assisted venous return) to keep venous pressure acceptable.
Venous pressure should, therefore, be kept close to zero, and certainly not more than 10 mmHg, to minimize increases in extracellular fluid.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 50

choiceNotes.d: Venous pressure should be **close to zero** and certainly not more than 10 mmHg.
choiceNotes.a: There is **no apparent physiologic advantage** to a CVP above zero; raising it needs more volume and often more prime.
choiceNotes.b: The **largest** venous cannulae compatible with the situation are used, lying **loosely, not snugly**.
choiceNotes.c: Venous pressure is a function of flow; with small cannulae, **reducing** flow (or applying venous suction) lowers it.

questions.topic: Changes During CPB: Pulmonary Venous Pressure
questions.stem: During total CPB, left atrial pressure monitoring shows **rising pulmonary venous pressure**. Which decompression method is effective?

choices.text: Suction via a catheter in the pulmonary trunk
Increasing arterial pump flow to the patient
Lowering plasma colloid osmotic pressure with crystalloid
More vacuum on the venous reservoir via the caval cannulae
Waiting until the pressure exceeds 20 mmHg

explanation.text: The pulmonary venous system can be decompressed by suction on a catheter (or opening) ==in the pulmonary trunk, because pulmonary veins have no valves==, or by a catheter in the left atrium or left ventricle.

explanation.title: Not a guarantee
explanation.text: Maintaining a very low pulmonary venous pressure **will not always** eliminate these complications.

the pulmonary venous system can be decompressed by suction on either a catheter (or an opening) in the pulmonary trunk, because no valves are present in pulmonary veins, or a catheter inside the left atrium or left ventricle.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 51

choiceNotes.d: Venous vacuum drains **systemic** venous return; pulmonary venous decompression uses the pulmonary trunk, left atrium, or left ventricle.
choiceNotes.e: Pulmonary venous pressure should ideally be **zero** and certainly not more than **10 mmHg**; lung water rises with the duration of elevation.
choiceNotes.b: Raising arterial flow over venous return **increases** atrial filling pressures.
choiceNotes.c: By the Starling law, a lower plasma colloid osmotic pressure favors **more** fluid moving out of the capillaries.

questions.stem: During core cooling, blood entering the aorta is kept **no more than 10°C–14°C below** the nasopharyngeal temperature. What is the reason?

choices.text: To prevent red cell aggregation in cold, sluggish flow
To limit gas coming out of solution on warming
To keep Tygon tubing from losing its elasticity
To limit the oxygen transfer demand on the oxygenator
To prevent blood damage at the heat exchanger surface

explanation.text: Cold blood warmed by the patient tends to ==release dissolved gas==; keeping arterial blood no more than **10°C–14°C** below nasopharyngeal temperature minimizes this.
This is a **conservative** recommendation: some groups use the coldest perfusate obtainable (**4°C–5°C**) once CPB is started.

blood entering the patient’s aorta should be kept no greater than 10°C to 14°C below the nasopharyngeal temperature to minimize the tendency for gas to come out of solution when the cold blood is warmed by the patient.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 51

choiceNotes.e: Heat-exchanger blood damage concerns temperatures **above 42°C** during rewarming.
choiceNotes.a: Rouleaux are addressed by a **lower hematocrit** at low temperature, not by this gradient.
choiceNotes.c: Tygon stiffening is managed by using **silicone rubber** tubing in the pump head.
choiceNotes.d: Maximal oxygenator demand occurs during **rewarming**, not cooling.

questions.stem: During **rewarming** on CPB, which statement about the heat exchanger and gas in the blood is correct?

choices.text: Water may exceed 42°C, since only blood temperature matters at the wall
An exchanger-to-blood gradient of up to 20°C avoids bubble formation
A downstream heat exchanger may need a bubble trap in the arterial tubing
An upstream heat exchanger is the position that risks bubble formation
Warming the blood increases the solubility of gas within it

explanation.text: Warming ==lowers gas solubility== in blood. This is not a problem with the heat exchanger **upstream** of the oxygenator, but **downstream** it is a potential problem, and a **bubble trap** may be interposed in the arterial tubing downstream to both.

head: Heat exchanger position
During rewarming
rows: Potential bubble problem -> **bubble trap** in the arterial tubing

steps.label: and
steps.text: The boundary layer at the exchanger wall probably reaches the **wall (water) temperature**

explanation.title: Gradient rule
explanation.text: In general, a heat exchanger-to-blood temperature gradient of **not more than 10°C–12°C** prevents bubble formation.
Solubility of gas in blood is decreased when blood is warmed, but this is not a problem when the heat exchanger is upstream (proximal) to the oxygenator.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 51

choiceNotes.d: Decreased gas solubility on warming is **not a problem** when the heat exchanger is **upstream** (proximal) to the oxygenator.

explanation.text: Were CPB started in a **nonheparinized** patient, the ==contact phase and intrinsic phase would be rapidly activated==, and within a short time the **pump-oxygenator would be filled with clot**.

explanation.title: Even with heparin
explanation.text: Heparin blocks the cascade **incompletely**: small amounts of fibrin form even during routine CPB, and many soluble coagulation factors are only **mildly reduced** by the end of CPB.

Heparin is therefore an **agent of damage**: an imperfect anticoagulant that permits microthrombi that can embolize. Many soluble coagulation factors are only **mildly reduced** by the end of CPB. In rare instances, heparin also produces adverse effects such as **severe thrombocytopenia**.
Were CPB to be started in a nonheparinized patient, the contact phase and intrinsic phase would be rapidly activated, and within a short time, the pump-oxygenator would be filled with clot.

choiceNotes.e: The **contact and intrinsic** phases would be rapidly activated, and within a short time the pump-oxygenator would be filled with clot.

questions.stem: During hypothermic low-flow CPB, cerebral oxygen consumption is measured **below the normal value for that temperature**. What does this imply?

choices.text: Incomplete or uneven perfusion of the cerebral capillary bed
Cerebral vasodilatation from CO~2~ added for pH-stat management
Excess cerebral oxygen delivery from a high perfusion flow rate
Luxury cerebral perfusion with a narrowed arteriovenous O~2~ difference
A normal adaptation, because cerebral V̇O~2~ falls with temperature

explanation.text: Cerebral V̇O~2~ **below the normal value at a given temperature** implies **incomplete or uneven cerebral perfusion** (decreased effective capillary density).
The normal relation between cerebral V̇O~2~ and nasopharyngeal temperature during full-flow CPB (2.0 L/min/m^2^) is described by a van’t Hoff equation (Fig. 2.16), presumably applicable to all ages.

explanation.title: Independent of cerebral blood flow
explanation.text: Cerebral V̇O~2~ does not appear to change with the variations in cerebral blood flow that occur during clinical CPB. In monkeys at 20°C it was the same at 0.5 and 1.6 L/min/m^2^, although cerebral blood flow at 0.5 was 50% of that at 1.6.

explanation.title: Wrong baseline
explanation.text: Do not assume cerebral V̇O~2~ at 37°C before CPB equals that at 37°C on CPB: whole-body V̇O~2~ on CPB is slightly less than off CPB, perhaps from uneven perfusion.
cerebral V̇O~2~ that is reduced below the usual (normal) value at a given temperature implies incomplete or uneven cerebral perfusion (decreased effective capillary density).
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 58

choiceNotes.d: Luxury perfusion is cerebral **blood flow** that is excessive relative to cerebral oxygen consumption, not a low consumption for the temperature.
choiceNotes.e: The comparison is already made **at the given temperature**; a value below the normal value for that temperature is abnormal.
choiceNotes.b: pH-stat CO~2~ causes cerebral vasodilatation (more flow); the source links a low cerebral V̇O~2~ for the temperature to incomplete or uneven perfusion.
choiceNotes.c: A low cerebral V̇O~2~ for the temperature points to **incomplete perfusion**, not excess delivery.

questions.stem: Despite adequate flow rates during CPB, a mild metabolic acidosis develops. What is its most probable cause according to the source?

choices.text: Endotoxin released by bacterial translocation from the gut
Accelerated lipolysis and proteolysis from the stress response
Underperfused areas from uneven distribution of flow
Addition of CO~2~ to the oxygenator gas for pH-stat management
Hemoglobin casts impairing renal tubular excretion of acid

explanation.text: Metabolic acidosis on CPB is probably related to **uneven distribution of flow**, with **underperfused areas releasing lactic acid**, even when flow rates are adequate.

steps.text: Usually mild metabolic acidosis (lactate rarely above 5 mmol/L)

explanation.text: Blood flow distribution on CPB **cannot be assumed** to be like that of the intact circulation; it may vary with age, hemodilution, flow, arterial pulse contour, drugs, temperatures, and arterial PCO~2~, pH and PO~2~.

explanation.title: Not only CPB
explanation.text: Sublingual microcirculatory alterations occurred with cardiac surgery **with or without CPB** and correlated with peak lactate; changes in the microcirculation cannot be attributed entirely to CPB.
Metabolic acidosis tends to develop during CPB, even when adequate flow rates are used.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 59

choiceNotes.d: Added CO~2~ for pH-stat management is described for its effect on **cerebral blood flow**, not as the cause of metabolic acidosis.
choiceNotes.e: Hemoglobin casts may form when plasma free hemoglobin exceeds about 40 mg/dL; they are not linked to the acidosis.
choiceNotes.a: Endotoxin stimulates complement, endothelial activation and TNF release; it is not the explanation given for acidosis.
choiceNotes.b: Lipolysis and proteolysis provide fuel and amino acids in the metabolic response to stress.

Abrupt rise at onset, then a gradual fall to below normal levels
No change at onset, then a steady progressive fall
Gradual fall throughout, lowest at the end of CPB

explanation.text: There is **considerable patient-to-patient variation** in SVR, and thus in arterial pressure, during perfusion; precise mechanisms are not identified except in one situation (reperfusion after global myocardial ischemia).

questions.stem: After a protracted period of global myocardial ischemia, the aortic clamp is released and cardiac reperfusion begins. Within about 30 to 45 seconds, systemic arterial pressure and resistance fall. What is the most likely explanation?

Sudden loss of venous tone as catecholamines are withdrawn
A rapid rise in bradykinin caused by systemic hypothermia
An adverse reaction to protamine at reperfusion
Release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla

explanation.text: Coronary sinus blood first appearing after appreciable global ischemia likely contains **vasodilating substances** formed in the heart; the **30 to 45 s** delay matches its transit through the circuit.

steps.text: Fall in arterial pressure and SVR
steps.label: about 30 to 45 s

explanation.text: Some studies suggest that this blood also contains a large number of **leukocytes** sequestered in the heart during global myocardial ischemia.

choiceNotes.d: Protamine is given **after terminating CPB**; the 30 to 45 s delay matches transit of coronary sinus blood through the circuit.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man with diffuse coronary disease is undergoing CABG, and the ascending aorta is suspected to be **severely atherosclerotic**. Which approach is recommended?

choices.text: Standard cannulation, since atheroma is an uncommon cause of postoperative stroke
Epiaortic ultrasound to site cannulae and clamps where disease is minimal
TEE alone, since it is the tool used to choose the clamp and cannulation sites
Repeated palpation of the aorta to map the plaques before clamping
Routine femoral cannulation, because retrograde perfusion avoids embolization

explanation.text: With advanced atherosclerosis, **epiaortic ultrasonographic scanning** is prudent to put **cannulae and clamps** where disease is **minimal or absent**.

head: Tool
Main role in this section
rows: Essential for monitoring **cardiac function** and detecting **intracardiac air**
Identifies aortic **plaques and calcification** to find optimal **clamping and cannulation sites**
explanation.caption: Two different ultrasound jobs

items: Off-pump coronary revascularization
On-CPB **beating-heart** revascularization with **peripheral cannulation** and **no aortic clamping**
Minimize manipulation of the atheromatous aorta

explanation.text: In patients with advanced arterial atherosclerosis, performing epiaortic ultrasonographic scanning of the aorta is prudent to detect severe arteriosclerosis and position cannulae and clamps in areas where arteriosclerotic disease is minimal or absent.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 67

choiceNotes.c: TEE is essential for monitoring cardiac function and detecting intracardiac air; **epiaortic ultrasound** identifies plaques and calcification to choose clamp and cannulation sites.
choiceNotes.d: Manipulation of the atheromatous aorta should be **minimized** to prevent atheroembolism.
choiceNotes.e: **Retrograde embolization** of debris from femoral artery cannulation is a well-recognized phenomenon.
choiceNotes.a: Brain embolism from atherosclerotic plaque is **one of the major causes** of new postoperative stroke after cardiac surgery.

questions.stem: After sternotomy, a baseline ACT is obtained in an adult about to undergo CPB. Which heparinization sequence is recommended **before cannulation**?

choices.text: Heparin 300 to 400 units/kg, then cannulate only when ACT is >480 s in every patient
Heparin added only to the pump prime (3 units/mL), with no dose given to the patient
Heparin 300 to 400 units/kg; recheck ACT at 3 to 5 min; top up to >400 s
Heparin 100 units/kg, repeat ACT after 3 to 5 minutes, then cannulate once ACT is >250 s
Heparin 300 to 400 units/kg, then cannulate at once without rechecking the ACT

explanation.text: Give **300 to 400 units/kg** (3 to 4 mg/kg), recheck the ACT at **3 to 5 minutes**, top up to an ACT **>400 s**, and **then cannulate**.

explanation.title: The prime gets heparin too
explanation.text: Heparin **3 units/mL** is added to the priming volume (for example, 5000 units for a 1600-mL clear prime).
Additional heparin is given as needed to achieve an ACT of greater than 400 seconds. Cannulation is then performed.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 67

choiceNotes.d: The dose is **300 to 400 units/kg** and the target ACT is **greater than 400 seconds**.
choiceNotes.e: The ACT is determined again **after 3 to 5 minutes**, and more heparin is given if needed before cannulation.
choiceNotes.a: An ACT **>480 s** is the target during **hypothermic** CPB (below 30°C); before cannulation the target is >400 s.
choiceNotes.b: Heparin in the prime (3 units/mL) is **in addition** to the patient dose of 300 to 400 units/kg.

choices.text: ACT greater than 480 seconds, checked only before weaning from CPB
ACT greater than 300 seconds, checked every 30 minutes
ACT greater than 400 seconds, checked every 2 hours
ACT greater than 480 seconds, checked every 30 minutes
ACT greater than 400 seconds, checked every 30 minutes

explanation.text: During **hypothermic** CPB (below 30°C) keep the ACT **>480 s**; check it **every 30 minutes**.

ACT target
Check

explanation.title: Poor response
explanation.text: The ACT should be measured **more frequently** if it does not respond appropriately to additional heparin; aprotinin and other factors can interfere with ACT interpretation, particularly with Celite.
additional heparin is given to maintain the ACT at greater than 400 seconds during normothermic CPB and at greater than 480 seconds during hypothermic CPB

choiceNotes.e: >400 s is the target during **normothermic** CPB; below 30°C the target is >480 s.
choiceNotes.a: Once CPB is established, the ACT is determined **every 30 minutes**.
choiceNotes.b: The targets are >400 s (normothermic) and **>480 s (hypothermic)**; 300 s is too low.
choiceNotes.c: Both the target (>480 s when hypothermic) and the interval (**every 30 minutes**) are wrong.

questions.stem: At the end of CPB, protamine sulfate is about to be given. Which statement about protamine is correct?

choices.text: It is given before the venous and arterial cannulae are removed
Its long duration of action makes heparin rebound impossible
It is a synthetic, high-molecular-weight polymer
It neutralizes heparin by forming covalent bonds with it
Fish allergy or prior NPH insulin exposure predisposes to anaphylaxis

explanation.text: **Fish allergy** or prior **NPH insulin** exposure → risk of **anaphylaxis** after protamine.

children: Complex partly metabolized or reacts with fibrinolysin
End of CPB, after all cannulae removed

choiceNotes.c: Protamine is a **biological product from salmon sperm** and a **simple protein of low molecular weight**.
choiceNotes.d: The heparin-protamine complex is based on **electrostatic attraction** (anionic heparin, cationic protamine).
choiceNotes.a: Protamine is given at the end of CPB **after removal of all cannulae**.
choiceNotes.b: The complex may be partially metabolized or react with fibrinolysin, **freeing heparin** and causing heparin **rebound**.

questions.stem: A patient received a total of **30,000 units** of heparin during the operation. Using the widely used fixed-ratio method, what protamine dose is given after CPB?

choices.text: About 300 to 450 mg
About 350 mg exactly, with no excess beyond neutralization
About 600 to 900 mg
About 30 to 45 mg
About 150 to 225 mg

explanation.text: **1 to 1.5 mg protamine per 100 units** of heparin: 30,000 units → **300 to 450 mg**.

explanation.title: Why more than the neutralizing amount?
explanation.text: 1 mg neutralizes about **85 units**, yet extra is given to prevent **heparin rebound** (heparin released from tissue stores or heparin-protamine aggregates) and to compensate for protamine's probable **shorter biological half-life**.

Key disadvantage

No correlation between ACT and heparin levels
Less protamine given; not reliant on ACT
Less protamine than fixed dose; decreased postoperative bleeding

explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 67

choiceNotes.d: The ratio is 1 to 1.5 mg per **100 units**, not per 1000 units.
choiceNotes.e: This is only half the dose given by 1 to 1.5 mg per 100 units.
choiceNotes.b: Extra protamine is **deliberately** given to prevent heparin rebound and to cover protamine's probable shorter half-life.
choiceNotes.c: This is double the dose given by 1 to 1.5 mg per 100 units.

questions.stem: After heparinization, an adult's ascending aorta is cannulated through the purse strings. Which step is correct?

choices.text: Make the stab wound before placing purse strings, to reduce bleeding
Only 5 to 10 mm of the cannula should project into the aorta
Advance the cannula so that 3 to 4 cm lies within the aortic lumen
Remove all clamps from the arterial tubing when a centrifugal pump is used
Connect the cannula to the arterial tubing without de-airing, since the line is primed

explanation.text: Care is taken that only **5 to 10 mm** of the aortic cannula projects into the aorta.

steps.text: Incise adventitia within the purse string
Digitally controlled **stab wound** (aorta steadied under the left index finger)
Insert cannula: **5 to 10 mm** inside; angled tip → **distal arch**
Secure tourniquet, tie cannula to it
Connect and **carefully de-air** the arterial line

head: Arterial pump
Clamps on arterial tubing after connection
explanation.caption: Pump type matters

explanation.text: Care is taken to adjust the cannula so that only 5 to 10 mm projects into the aorta. If an angled cannula is used, it is positioned so that the opening faces distally into the aortic arch.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 68

choiceNotes.c: Care is taken that **only 5 to 10 mm** projects into the aorta.
choiceNotes.d: Clamps are removed if a **roller pump** is used, but **not** if the arterial pump is of the controlled vortex (centrifugal) type.
choiceNotes.e: The arterial cannula is connected to the arterial tubing and **carefully de-aired**.
choiceNotes.a: The adventitia **within the purse string** is incised and the stab wound is made within it.

questions.stem: In an infant with a **large heart**, direct caval cannulation is planned, but each attempt to expose the IVC causes severe hypotension. What is the recommended approach?

choices.text: Proceed to circulatory arrest without venous cannulation
Keep retracting the heart and accept brief hypotension until the IVC cannula is in
Cannulate the SVC first, start partial CPB, then expose and cannulate the IVC
Cannulate the IVC first, then establish full CPB before placing the SVC cannula
Cannulate the femoral vein, since peripheral cannulation suits very small patients

explanation.text: When IVC exposure is difficult, **cannulate the SVC first**, start **partial CPB**, and **then** expose and cannulate the IVC.

steps.text: Large heart in a neonate or infant
Then IVC tape, purse string, and cannula

explanation.title: How low in weight?
explanation.text: Two venous cannulae inserted directly into the cavae are well suited for children, infants, and neonates down to about **2.5 kg**; drainage can be verified by **SVC pressure** from a small internal jugular catheter.

When exposure of the IVC is particularly difficult, the SVC may be cannulated first, partial CPB established, and the IVC then exposed for placing the tape and purse-string suture and for inserting the cannula.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 68

choiceNotes.d: The source cannulates the **SVC first**, because exposing the IVC is the difficult, hypotension-provoking step.
choiceNotes.e: In **very small patients**, peripheral cannulation is **not practical**.
choiceNotes.a: The source's solution is **SVC cannulation and partial CPB**, after which the IVC is exposed.
choiceNotes.b: These exposure maneuvers can lead to **severe** hypotension; the source avoids them by starting partial CPB first.

questions.stem: After direct cannulation of both venae cavae for an intracardiac repair, how must the cannula tips lie to avoid **venous obstruction**?

choices.text: SVC tip pointing downward and IVC tip pointing upward
Both tips crossed in the mid-right atrium
Both tips pointing toward the right atrium to collect atrial blood
Parallel to the caval walls; SVC tip upward, IVC tip downward
Perpendicular to the caval walls to maximize the inflow area

explanation.text: Each caval cannula tip lies **parallel to the caval wall**: **SVC tip up**, **IVC tip down**; otherwise venous obstruction results.

explanation.title: Getting it right every time
explanation.text: Attach the cannulae to the **Y connector** on the venous line in exactly the right orientation **before** insertion.

explanation.title: Check the result
explanation.text: Drainage can be verified by **routine SVC pressure measurement** through a small catheter placed earlier in the **internal jugular vein**.
After the cannulae are inserted, each tip must lie directly parallel to the walls of the vena cava, with the tip of the SVC cannula pointing upward and that of the IVC downward.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 68

choiceNotes.c: The SVC tip points **upward** and the IVC tip **downward**, away from the atrium.
choiceNotes.e: Each tip must lie **directly parallel** to the walls of the vena cava.
choiceNotes.a: This is the reverse of the recommended orientation.
choiceNotes.b: Mid-right atrial **side holes** belong to the single two-stage cannula, not to direct caval cannulae.

The cardiac chambers must be closed before rewarming starts
Direct caval cannulation is suitable only for patients above 10 kg
SVC pressure cannot be monitored once the cavae are cannulated
The IVC cannula may need moving into the right atrium after the heart is closed

explanation.text: Disadvantage: once the heart is closed, the **IVC cannula** may have to be moved **into the right atrium** so it is not distended by **coronary sinus and SVC** return.

Disadvantage
rows: Heart **opened and exposure arranged during late cooling**, before arrest
After closure, IVC cannula may need **repositioning into the right atrium**
Otherwise the atrium distends with coronary sinus and/or SVC blood

explanation.text: A disadvantage is that when the heart is closed, the inferior caval cannula may have to be repositioned into the right atrium to prevent its distention by blood returning from the coronary sinus, SVC, or both.

questions.topic: Commencing CPB and Left Heart Venting
questions.stem: A neonate is placed on CPB with a **cold prime** (18°C to 22°C). What should the team anticipate as bypass begins?

choices.text: Heart rate slows and contraction is impaired; full pump flow is needed rapidly
Ventricular distention cannot occur because the cold heart is stiff
The heart's contribution to total flow rises, so pump flow can be increased slowly
Myocardial function is unaffected until the nasopharyngeal temperature falls below 25°C
Heart rate rises and contraction becomes more vigorous for several minutes

explanation.text: A **cold prime** immediately slows and weakens the heart, so its share of flow falls fast: the **arterial pump must reach full flow rapidly**.

steps.text: Heart's contribution to total flow **rapidly diminishes**
Arterial pump must **rapidly reach full flow**

explanation.title: Watch the ventricle
explanation.text: Neonates and infants have **high ventricular compliance** and a heart **less tolerant of excessive preload**; watch for distention.
If a cold prime is used, myocardial function is immediately affected after establishing CPB. Heart rate slows, and contraction is impaired.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.c: With a cold prime the heart's contribution **rapidly diminishes**, so the pump must reach full flow **rapidly**.
choiceNotes.d: Myocardial function is affected **immediately** after establishing CPB with a cold prime.
choiceNotes.e: Heart rate **slows** and contraction is **impaired**.
choiceNotes.b: The heart must be watched for **ventricular distention**, especially in infants and neonates with high ventricular compliance.
