questions.stem: Shortly after CPB is commenced in an infant, the heart is seen to become **distended**. What should be done?

choices.text: Add cold prime to slow the heart further
Reduce pump flow and reposition the venous cannulae
Increase pump flow to unload the ventricle
Stop the pump until the heart has emptied
Stop ventilation at once, whatever the cardiac contractility

explanation.text: Distention on initiation → **reduce pump flow** and **reposition the venous cannulae**.

explanation.title: Why infants are at risk
explanation.text: Infants and neonates have **high ventricular compliance** and a heart **less tolerant of excessive preload**.
If distention occurs, pump flow must be reduced and the venous cannulae repositioned.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.c: If distention occurs, pump flow must be **reduced**, not increased.
choiceNotes.d: Distention is managed by **reducing** pump flow and **repositioning the venous cannulae**, not by stopping the pump.
choiceNotes.e: If contractility is maintained, it is preferable to **maintain ventilation** until full flow is achieved.
choiceNotes.a: Cold prime impairs contraction; the remedy for distention is **lower flow and venous cannula repositioning**.

questions.topic: Commencing CPB and Left Heart Venting
questions.stem: In an adult, a left-heart vent is to be inserted through a purse string at the junction of the right superior pulmonary vein and left atrium while the heart is **beating** and the aorta is **not clamped**. Which maneuver reduces the risk of cerebral air embolism?

choices.text: Advance the catheter blindly, without palpating its tip
Make the purse string large enough to encircle the pulmonary vein orifice
Increase venous pressure by reducing venous drainage, so the heart fills with blood
Maximize venous drainage to empty the heart before the incision
Insert the vent through the pulmonary trunk, which decompresses best

explanation.text: In a **beating** heart with the aorta **unclamped**, air introduced during vent insertion can **embolize to the brain**; therefore venous drainage is **reduced** to raise venous pressure and the **blood volume in the heart** before the incision.

steps.text: Purse string: atrial wall + pulmonary vein adventitia (orifice spared)
Palpate tip from behind the heart → through **mitral valve** into LV

explanation.title: Left heart vent via right superior pulmonary vein
Same risk on the way out
explanation.text: The same precautions against air are needed when the vent is **withdrawn** at the end of the operation.
This must be done precisely if the heart is beating because air can be introduced into it and embolize to the brain unless the aorta has been clamped.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.d: The source does the opposite: venous pressure is **increased by reducing venous drainage**, to increase blood volume in the heart.
choiceNotes.e: With the pulmonary trunk, drainage and decompression of the left heart **may be suboptimal**.
choiceNotes.a: The left hand is placed **behind the heart** to palpate the tip and guide it through the mitral valve.
choiceNotes.b: The stitch **should not** be large enough to compromise the pulmonary vein orifice when tied.

questions.stem: For tricuspid valve surgery with two caval cannulae, the right atrium is opened. The atrial septum is **intact** (no PFO or ASD), and the left heart is to be vented with a sump catheter placed across the septum. Where is the stab wound made?

choices.text: In the inferior fossa ovalis, close to the IVC orifice
Anywhere along the interatrial groove
Through the anterior limbus near the aortic root
In the fossa ovalis, directly beneath the superior limbus
In the coronary sinus ostium

explanation.text: Without a PFO or ASD, stab the **fossa ovalis directly beneath the superior limbus**; otherwise the vent may end up **outside the heart**.

explanation.title: A two-chamber sump

explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.e: The coronary sinus ostium is a site for picking up **left SVC** flow, not for entering the left atrium.
choiceNotes.a: The landmark is the **superior limbus**; an imprecise stab wound may place the vent **outside the heart**.
choiceNotes.b: An imprecisely made stab wound may leave the vent **outside the heart** rather than in the left atrium.
choiceNotes.c: The stab wound is made **directly beneath the superior limbus**, in the fossa ovalis.

explanation.text: A broad range of temperatures can be used, but in most cases the nasopharyngeal temperature should be lowered to ==at least 32°C==; **below this level, perfusion flow rate can be safely reduced**.

Hold the nasopharynx at 37°C for about 10 minutes, to limit downward drift after bypass
Wean from CPB as rewarming begins, and complete warming after bypass

explanation.text: It is **advantageous but not essential** to have the **nasopharyngeal** temperature at **37°C for about 10 minutes** before CPB is discontinued, to avoid **excessive downward temperature drift** after bypass.

choiceNotes.c: Rewarming is completed **on CPB**: CPB is discontinued when the nasopharyngeal temperature has reached 37°C.

questions.stem: As the cardiac chambers are being closed after an open-heart repair, the team prepares to de-air the heart. Which is one of the **established principles** of de-airing?

choices.text: Stop aortic vent suction as soon as the heart begins to eject
Keep the heart arrested and empty while air is removed
Fill the heart with blood or electrolyte solution before closing it
Keep the lungs deflated throughout so that no air is pushed into the heart
Allow the heart to eject first, then aspirate any remaining air

explanation.text: Principle 1 of de-airing: **fill the heart with fluid** (blood or electrolyte solution) **before closing** it, to minimize air entrapment.

items: **Fill** the heart with fluid before closing
Heart **reperfused and beating**
**Aspirate** residual air **before** the heart ejects
**Intermittently ventilate** the lungs to express air from the pulmonary veins
**Continuous suction** on an ascending aortic needle vent (or a freely bleeding stab wound) as ejection begins

explanation.title: Why it matters
explanation.text: Clinical studies show a **correlation between the number of gaseous microemboli and the severity of neuropsychological impairment** after CPB.
The heart is filled with fluid (blood or electrolyte solution) before closing to minimize air entrapment.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 69

choiceNotes.d: The lungs are **intermittently ventilated** to express air from the pulmonary veins.
choiceNotes.e: Residual air is aspirated **before** allowing the heart to eject.
choiceNotes.a: **Continuous suction** is applied on the aortic needle vent as the heart commences ejecting.
choiceNotes.b: The heart must be **reperfused and beating**, and filled with fluid.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: During de-airing at the end of an **aortic valve replacement**, which step follows the technique described?

choices.text: Raise perfusion flow as the aortic clamp is released
Remove the aortic needle vent as soon as the heart starts to eject
Inflate the lungs vigorously while the aortotomy is still open
Needle-aspirate the LV through the front of its apex
Tilt the table head-up before slowly releasing the aortic clamp

explanation.text: Needle aspiration through the **front of the LV apex** removes the air pocket that is **almost always present** there.

steps.text: Fill heart; inject fluid if blood does not escape from the aortotomy; **gentle** lung inflation
Aspirate the **LA dome**; invert the LA appendage
Aspirate the **LV apex** (heart pulled forward and to the right)
Release clamp slowly with **reduced flow**; aspirate the aortic needle vent
Remove LA vent, defibrillate if needed, shake the LV; heart ejects as CVP rises to 10 mmHg
Level the table; remove the aortic vent **last**

explanation.title: Do not hurry
explanation.text: These maneuvers should not be hurried; the aortic needle vent should not be removed until the heart has been ejecting well **for some time**.
This is a simple and effective way of removing the pocket of air that is almost always present at this site.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 70

choiceNotes.c: Inflation must be **gentle**: when the lungs collapse, air can be drawn into the LV through the **still-opened aorta**.
choiceNotes.e: The table is tilted with the patient's **head down**.
choiceNotes.a: Perfusion flow is **temporarily reduced** as the clamp is slowly released, and LV overdistention must be prevented.
choiceNotes.b: The **longer** the aortic needle vent is in use, the better; it stays until the heart has been ejecting well for some time.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: Which statement about **TEE** in removing air from the heart before CPB is discontinued is supported?

choices.text: It has been shown conclusively to improve outcomes when standard de-airing is used
It detects only large collections of intracardiac air
It replaces the need for a strict de-airing protocol
Small amounts of intracardiac air it detects carry a high risk of damage
It is of particular value with small incisions or limited left heart mobilization

explanation.text: TEE is **of particular value** with **small incisions**, when the left heart is **not fully mobilized**, or when usual maneuvers (LV aspiration and manipulation) **cannot be used**.

head: Statement
Verdict
rows: Detects even small amounts of intracardiac and intraaortic air
Clinical benefit with standard de-airing proven
Small amounts of air are dangerous
**Small incisions**, limited mobilization, no LV aspiration/manipulation
explanation.caption: TEE and de-airing

explanation.title: Protocol first
explanation.text: Adherence to a **strict protocol** for removal of air suffices for most patients.
However, TEE is of particular value during operations employing small incisions, when the left-sided cardiac chambers are not fully mobilized, or when some of the usual maneuvers for removal of air
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 70

choiceNotes.a: The clinical benefit of TEE with standard de-airing procedures **has not been conclusively demonstrated**.
choiceNotes.b: TEE identifies **even small amounts** of intracardiac and intraaortic air.
choiceNotes.c: A **strict protocol** for removing air will suffice for most patients; TEE is commonly used to monitor it.
choiceNotes.d: Small amounts of intracardiac air have a **low probability** of causing detectable damage.

questions.stem: CO~2~ is used to flood the operative field during a **reoperative** valve procedure. Which statement about this technique is correct?

choices.text: Arterial blood gases and electrolytes must be monitored frequently
A high-velocity jet into the wound gives the most efficient de-airing
It works because CO~2~ is lighter than air and rises out of the heart
CO~2~ emboli are less well tolerated than air emboli
A CO~2~ flow of about 0.5 L·min^-1^ is enough to de-air the wound

explanation.text: CO~2~ flooding can cause **profound systemic hypercarbia and acidosis**, so **arterial blood gases and electrolytes** must be monitored frequently.

children: RCT, single valve surgery: **fewer microemboli** on TEE in LA, LV, ascending aorta

explanation.text: CO2 may have an important role in operations performed through small incisions or during reoperative procedures, but the potential for inducing profound systemic hypercarbia and acidosis exists.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 70

choiceNotes.c: CO~2~ displaces air because it is a **heavier** gas.
choiceNotes.d: CO~2~ emboli, if they occur, are **better tolerated** than air emboli.
choiceNotes.e: In vitro, the flow should be about **5 L·min^-1^** to compensate for diffusion with ambient air.
choiceNotes.b: Outflow velocity should be about **0.1 m·sec^-1^ or less** to avoid turbulence in the wound.

questions.stem: A patient has just had a **mechanical aortic valve** implanted and will be anticoagulated. Which statement about needle-type right ventricular pacing wires, compared with epicardial wires, is correct?

choices.text: They are placed on the lateral wall of the right atrium
Lower, longer-lasting thresholds, but slightly more bleeding risk
They give higher pacing thresholds but carry a lower bleeding risk
They should be avoided when complete heart block follows reperfusion
Their bleeding risk is irrelevant when anticoagulants are given after surgery

explanation.text: Needle-type RV wires: **lower thresholds that last longer** (useful in complete heart block), but **slightly more bleeding**, which matters with **anticoagulation**.

head: Epicardial wires
Needle-type RV wires
rows: Usual wires, sutured to the myocardium
**Complete heart block** after reperfusion and rewarming
explanation.caption: Temporary ventricular pacing wires

explanation.text: Two temporary wires go on the **lateral wall of the right atrium**; one or two are sutured to the **right ventricle** (anterior or inferior surface).
However, the chances for bleeding at the time of wire placement and removal are slightly higher than with epicardial wires.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 70

choiceNotes.c: Needle-type wires give **lower** thresholds and a slightly **higher** bleeding risk.
choiceNotes.d: They are **useful** if the patient has complete heart block after reperfusion and rewarming.
choiceNotes.e: The bleeding risk is **particularly important** if the patient is anticoagulated (e.g., mechanical aortic valve).
choiceNotes.a: The **atrial** wires go on the lateral right atrial wall; needle-type wires are placed into the **right ventricular** wall.

questions.stem: After CPB through a median sternotomy, the pericardium is generally left open. What is an advantage of this practice?

choices.text: It is used only when the aorta or an aortic graft is prominent
It completely eliminates the risk of tamponade
It reduces the tendency of retained blood to raise intrapericardial pressure
It allows the mediastinal drainage tubes to be omitted
It lets blood collect around the heart to tamponade suture-line bleeding

explanation.text: An open pericardium **drains** mediastinal and substernal blood and **reduces** (not eliminates) the risk of **tamponade**.

items: **Good blood drainage** from mediastinal and substernal tissues into the pericardium (then out through the tubes) → **no hematomas** there
**Less positive intrapericardial pressure** from retained blood → less **tamponade**

explanation.title: Reoperation
explanation.text: Reoperations have **not posed a major problem** with this technique; a few sutures may cover a prominent aorta or aortic graft.
reduction (but not elimination) of the tendency of retained blood to produce a positive intrapericardial pressure
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.b: The tendency to positive intrapericardial pressure is **reduced, but not eliminated**.
choiceNotes.d: Blood drains into the pericardial cavity **and then out through the drainage tubes**.
choiceNotes.e: The advantage is **good drainage** that prevents hematomas, not retention of blood.
choiceNotes.a: A prominent aorta or graft is the situation where a **few sutures** may be placed at the upper end.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: At sternal closure, an elderly patient's sternal edges are **thin and fragmented**. Which technique is described?

choices.text: Absorbable sutures passed through the sternum in place of wires
Bone wax applied generously to consolidate the fragile edges
Leaving the sternum open for delayed closure
Vertical parasternal wires in front of and behind the costal cartilages
Wires tied in square knots rather than twisted, for a tighter closure

explanation.text: Thin or fragmented edges: **vertical parasternal wires** in front of and behind the **costal cartilages**, then incorporated into the **transverse** wires.

items: Cephalad 1 or 2 wires through the **manubrium**; next 3 or 4 through or around the sternum; lowest 1 or 2 through the sternum
Wires are **twisted, not tied**
**Sternal plating** may replace or supplement cerclage wires
Absorbable sutures for muscles and linea alba; skin subcuticular or staples

explanation.title: Fragile sternum
explanation.text: In older patients with a fragile sternum, **avoid bone wax** altogether.
If the sternal edges are thin or fragmented, wire sutures can be passed vertically in the parasternal position in front of and behind the costal cartilages on one or both sides.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.e: Stainless steel wires are **twisted, not tied**.
choiceNotes.a: Absorbable sutures close the **muscles and linea alba**; the sternum is closed with stainless steel wire (or plates).
choiceNotes.b: When the sternum is fragile, as in older patients, it is better to **avoid wax altogether**.
choiceNotes.c: Leaving the sternum open is for a **suboptimal hemodynamic state**, not for fragile bone.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: After a long operation, the patient's hemodynamic state is **suboptimal** as preparations are made to close the chest. What does the source recommend?

choices.text: Leave the sternum open but close the skin over it
Leave the sternum open and plan secondary closure after 7 to 10 days
Leave the sternum open, preferably covered by a sutured silicone rubber sheet
Close the sternum and support the heart with inotropes, as an open chest rarely helps
Leave the chest unsutured and plan secondary closure in 24 to 48 hours

explanation.text: With a **suboptimal hemodynamic state**, leave the chest **open** (sternum, subcutaneous tissue, skin) and close it **24 to 48 hours** later.

steps.label: instead
steps.text: Leave unsutured; **vacuum-assisted** wound care (or loose packing + adhesive sheet)

explanation.title: Lifesaving
explanation.text: This maneuver, regardless of technical details, is **lifesaving** in some patients.
Vacuum-assisted wound care systems have largely replaced the use of an impervious sheet of silicone rubber or bovine pericardium to temporarily cover the mediastinal structures.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.d: Closing the sternum **frequently further depresses cardiac function**; leaving it open is **lifesaving** in some patients.
choiceNotes.a: The sternum, subcutaneous tissue, **and skin** are all left unsutured.
choiceNotes.b: Secondary closure can usually be performed **24 to 48 hours** later.
choiceNotes.c: **Vacuum-assisted wound care** systems have largely replaced silicone rubber or bovine pericardium sheets.

questions.stem: Which statement about the components of the pump-oxygenator is correct?

choices.text: Integrated heat exchangers are less efficient but reduce priming volume
Priming volume should be cut by removing every possible component
Venous reservoirs substantially reduce the priming volume of the system
The arterial roller pump should be set fully occlusive
Bubble oxygenators are currently indicated for cardiac surgery

explanation.text: **Integrated** heat exchangers: **less efficient** than freestanding ones, but **lower priming volume**.

head: Component
Key point
rows: Lets **air escape** and **stores** excess volume (hard-shell type allows VAVR); **increases** priming volume
Most varied, most important, probably **most damaging**; microporous or true membrane
Integrated = **less efficient**, **less priming volume**; freestanding = more efficient
Roller pump set **slightly nonocclusive**, calibrated often; or centrifugal with ultrasonic flow measurement
explanation.caption: Pump-oxygenator components

explanation.title: Priming volume trade-off
explanation.text: Every component adds priming volume, but **oversimplifying** the system can compromise safety.
Integrated heat exchangers are generally less efficient than freestanding ones, but they reduce priming volume.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.c: Venous reservoirs, although useful, **substantially increase** priming volume.
choiceNotes.d: The roller pump should be adjusted before each perfusion to be **slightly nonocclusive** and calibrated at frequent intervals.
choiceNotes.e: **Microporous and true membrane** oxygenators have advantages over bubble oxygenators and are currently indicated.
choiceNotes.b: Systems can be so **oversimplified** to reduce priming volume that **safety may be compromised**.

questions.stem: During CPB, the arterial line pressure in the pump-oxygenator rises to **320 mmHg**. What is the main concern?

choices.text: It shows the roller pump is slightly nonocclusive and should be made fully occlusive
Increased risk of arterial line disruption and of cavitation near the arterial cannula
None; pressures up to 400 mmHg are acceptable with a roller pump
It suggests the arterial cannula is too large for the aorta
It indicates an air lock in the venous line

explanation.text: Arterial line pressure **above 250 to 300 mmHg** increases the risk of **line disruption** and **cavitation** at the arterial cannula.

explanation.title: Arterial pump set-up
explanation.text: Roller pump: adjusted to be **slightly nonocclusive** and **calibrated** often so flow is accurate. Centrifugal pump: use **ultrasonic flow measurement**.
When this pressure exceeds 250 to 300 mmHg, risk of disruption of the arterial line and cavitation in the region of the arterial cannula increases.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.c: Risk rises when arterial line pressure **exceeds 250 to 300 mmHg**.
choiceNotes.d: The source links proper arterial line pressure to a properly positioned cannula of **adequate size**; it does not describe a too-large cannula as the cause.
choiceNotes.e: An air lock stops **venous return** to the pump; it is not an arterial line pressure problem.
choiceNotes.a: The roller pump **should** be adjusted to be **slightly nonocclusive** before each perfusion.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: Which statement about a **low-porosity (40-µm) filter** in the arterial line is supported?

choices.text: A randomized CABG study showed better neuropsychiatric function only with the filter
Gaseous microemboli are more prevalent with membrane than with bubble oxygenators
It considerably reduces gaseous microemboli on transcranial Doppler studies
It is unnecessary with membrane oxygenators, which produce no gaseous microemboli
One filter type should be used everywhere, regardless of the other circuit components

explanation.text: 40-µm arterial filters **considerably reduce gaseous microemboli** on transcranial Doppler; **routine use appears beneficial**.

head: Evidence
Finding
rows: Good neuropsychiatric function **with or without** filter
explanation.caption: Arterial line filter

explanation.title: Still somewhat controversial
explanation.text: Advantages, disadvantages, and need for the filter remain **somewhat controversial**; the exact filter is chosen **within each institution**.
Currently, routine use of a low-porosity filter of this type in the arterial line appears to be beneficial.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 71

choiceNotes.a: Walker's randomized study showed **good** neuropsychiatric function **whether or not** a filter was present.
choiceNotes.b: Gaseous microemboli are **more prevalent with bubble** oxygenators.
choiceNotes.d: Microemboli are **less prevalent** (not absent) with membrane oxygenators, and routine filter use appears beneficial.
choiceNotes.e: The exact filter and its compatibility with other components must be **determined within each institution**.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: Which statement about **cardiotomy suction** in the CPB circuit is correct?

choices.text: A rapidly variable high-capacity vacuum system is the current standard
Aspirated blood can return to the circuit without filtration or defoaming
Blood may be left in the pericardium to reduce suction trauma
Blocking the open end of a roller-pump sucker rapidly raises suction
One cardiotomy suction port is generally sufficient

explanation.text: Roller-pump suckers: when the open end is **blocked, suction rises rapidly** and may damage **tissue or blood**, so **constant monitoring** is needed.

items: **At least two** cardiotomy suction ports
Blood passes a **low-porosity filter** and is **defoamed** in a separate chamber open to air
Aspirate pericardial blood **promptly** during the perfusion
Ideal: variable high-capacity vacuum; in practice: **roller pumps** with constant monitoring

explanation.text: With this system, when the open end of the line is blocked, the suction rapidly increases; this may damage either the tissue or the blood.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.b: This blood may contain particulate matter and air; it must pass a **low-porosity filter** and be **defoamed** before return.
choiceNotes.c: During the perfusion, blood should be **promptly aspirated** from the pericardium with the cardiotomy suckers.
choiceNotes.e: The circuit should generally contain **at least two** cardiotomy suction ports.
choiceNotes.a: Such a vacuum system would be ideal but has proved **impractical**, so **roller pumps** are used.

questions.stem: A **miniaturized extracorporeal circuit (MECC)** is chosen for CABG. Which feature defines this circuit?

choices.text: A hard-shell venous reservoir that allows vacuum-assisted venous return
An integral cardiotomy suction device returning shed blood
A roller pump with a microporous oxygenator, open to air
A bubble oxygenator chosen to minimize the priming volume
Closed and heparin-coated, with only a centrifugal pump and membrane oxygenator

explanation.text: MECC = **closed**, **heparin-coated** circuit: **centrifugal pump + membrane oxygenator** only; **no venous reservoir**, **no cardiotomy suction**.
These closed circuits with little or no blood/air contact have a controlled vortex (centrifugal) blood pump and a membrane oxygenator as the only components.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.a: MECC has **no venous reservoir**.
choiceNotes.b: MECC has **no integral cardiac suction device**.
choiceNotes.c: MECC circuits are **closed** with little or no blood/air contact and use a **centrifugal** pump.
choiceNotes.d: The oxygenator in MECC is a **membrane** oxygenator.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

questions.stem: A meta-analysis of randomized trials compared conventional CPB with **miniaturized CPB circuits** (mostly CABG patients). Which result was found?

choices.text: Fewer neurologic events and transfusions, lower troponin; same early mortality
No difference in any of the outcomes examined
Fewer neurologic events and lower mortality, but higher troponin
Lower early mortality, with no difference in the number of transfused patients
More neurologic events, offset by fewer patients needing transfusion

explanation.text: Miniaturized circuits: **fewer neurologic events**, **fewer transfused patients**, **lower peak troponin**; **early mortality unchanged**.

explanation.title: Nonrandomized CABG data also suggest
explanation.text: Fewer transfusions, less troponin release, **less postoperative atrial fibrillation**, **less acute kidney injury**, less thrombin generation, and lower IL-6 and SC5b-9.

miniaturized circuits are associated with substantial reductions in neurologic injury, number of patients requiring transfusion of blood products, and peak cardiac troponin release (Table 2.6). No difference in early mortality was noted.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.d: **No difference in early mortality** was noted; the number of transfused patients was **reduced**.
choiceNotes.e: Neurologic injury was **substantially reduced** with miniaturized circuits.
choiceNotes.b: Neurologic events, transfused patients, and peak troponin were **all reduced**.
choiceNotes.c: Peak troponin was **lower**, and mortality was **not different**.

questions.stem: During a repair **inside the right ventricle** using a single venous cannula without assisted venous return, venous return to the pump suddenly stops and blood floods the right heart. What should be done?

choices.text: Stop the pump until the right heart empties spontaneously
Maintain perfusion flow and keep the intracardiac sucker outside the heart
Reduce the perfusion flow rate until venous return recovers
Place the intracardiac sucker deep in the ventricle to aspirate the air
Withdraw the cannula tip from the IVC into the mid-right atrium

explanation.text: Air lock: **do not reduce perfusion flow**; keep the **sucker outside the heart** to control the pericardial well while the air lock is moved down into the **venous reservoir**.

steps.text: Operation in RV or pulmonary trunk, single cannula, no assisted venous return

steps.label: air enters RA via tricuspid valve

steps.text: Venous return stops abruptly; blood floods the right heart

steps.label: response
steps.text: Flow **unchanged**; sucker **outside** the heart; air lock expelled into the reservoir

explanation.title: When a single cannula is ideal
explanation.text: A single two-stage cannula is optimal for many adult operations and in neonates, infants, and children when the **entire repair** is done during **hypothermic circulatory arrest**.
The perfusionist must not reduce the perfusion flow rate, but instead, the intracardiac sucker is positioned outside the heart to keep blood from overflowing from the pericardial well
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 72

choiceNotes.c: The perfusionist **must not reduce** the perfusion flow rate.
choiceNotes.d: The sucker is positioned **outside the heart** to keep blood from overflowing the pericardial well.
choiceNotes.e: The principle remains: **tip in the IVC**, side holes in the right atrium.
choiceNotes.a: Flow is maintained while the air lock is **moved down the venous line** and expelled into the venous reservoir.

questions.stem: A patient with a severely atheromatous aorta needs arch surgery with antegrade cerebral perfusion. Axillary cannulation is planned, but there is atheroma at the **orifice of the brachiocephalic artery**. Which risk and strategy are described?

choices.text: Change to femoral cannulation, because retrograde perfusion carries no embolic risk
Begin full systemic perfusion first, then isolate the arch vessels
Atheroemboli from that lesion; start cerebral perfusion before systemic perfusion
Cannulate the ascending aorta instead, since antegrade aortic perfusion is always feasible
No embolic risk, because axillary perfusion is antegrade; proceed routinely

explanation.text: Axillary flow can dislodge atheroma at the **brachiocephalic orifice**; isolate the **arch vessels early** with cerebral perfusion **before systemic perfusion**.

steps.label: Shiiya
steps.text: ACP from **right and left axillary** arteries + **direct left common carotid** perfusion

head: Route
Embolic concern
rows: Preferred, but atheroma may preclude it
Emboli from atheroma at the **brachiocephalic orifice**
explanation.caption: Arterial routes in the atheromatous patient

explanation.text: Axillary arterial cannulation became a popular strategy; however, it is possible to cause atheroemboli from an atheromatous lesion at the orifice of the brachiocephalic artery.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 73

choiceNotes.e: Axillary cannulation **can** cause atheroemboli from an atheromatous lesion at the brachiocephalic orifice.
choiceNotes.a: **Retrograde embolization** by debris from femoral cannulation is a well-recognized phenomenon.
choiceNotes.b: Shiiya's approach starts cerebral perfusion **before** initiating systemic perfusion.
choiceNotes.d: An atheromatous aorta **sometimes precludes** ascending aortic cannulation.

questions.stem: For a high-risk **reoperation**, CPB is established through the groin before the sternum is reopened. The **left** femoral vein must be used for venous drainage. What is the recommended technique?

choices.text: Use a small (16F) cannula to limit injury to the vein
Insert the cannula without a guidewire, as is usual from the left side
Expose the vein above the inguinal ligament through a lower abdominal incision
Pass the cannula over a guidewire placed into the right atrium or IVC
Advance a short cannula only as far as the iliac vein

explanation.text: From the **left** femoral vein, a **guidewire** (tip in the right atrium or adjacent IVC) is often needed to pass the long cannula **over the sacral promontory into the IVC**.

head: Open technique
Seldinger technique
rows: Vertical or oblique groin-crease incision; below the inguinal ligament
Appropriate size, transverse arteriotomy between clamps
Large **28F to 32F**, long, into the IVC
Guidewire often needed from the left side
explanation.caption: Femoral cannulation

explanation.title: Why go peripheral first?
explanation.text: To establish CPB **before opening the sternum** in reoperations with a high probability of entering a cardiac chamber or major artery during sternotomy.

If the left femoral vein is used, it is often necessary to insert a guidewire, positioning the tip in the right atrium or the adjacent IVC, and then the venous cannula, which is inserted over the wire.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 73

choiceNotes.e: A large, **long** cannula must be advanced **over the sacral promontory into the IVC**.
choiceNotes.a: A **large (28F to 32F)** long cannula is used with open femoral cannulation.
choiceNotes.b: From the **right** femoral vein this is usually easy; from the **left** a guidewire is often necessary.
choiceNotes.c: A groin-crease incision is used, working **inferiorly** from the inguinal ligament to the common femoral vessels.

questions.stem: A patient with an existing **aortic dissection** needs peripheral arterial cannulation, and the axillary artery is chosen instead of the femoral artery. Which is a listed advantage of axillary cannulation?

choices.text: Exposure carries no risk to the brachial plexus
Cannulation can be performed without systemic heparin
It needs no incision because it is always done percutaneously
Proximal and distal control of the artery is not needed
It avoids malperfusion from retrograde femoral flow

explanation.text: In an existing dissection, retrograde femoral flow may cause **central malperfusion**; axillary cannulation offers **absence of malperfusion**, **brain blood flow** during otherwise whole-body arrest, and presumably no **retrograde particulate embolization**.

steps.text: Transverse incision **below the lateral two-thirds** of the clavicle
